# import matplotlib for plotting (like ggplot but isn't included in pandas)
import matplotlib.pyplot as plot

Next we want to start running an analysis. To do so we need to do a little bit of data cleaning. For this analysis we will focus on teams, conferences, and their win-loss record. The data luckily has all of this for us but not in the correct format. Like in R, we can use Regex to handle the data extraction. We will do this below to extract the conference from the team name (Team) and the win loss record (Win-Loss). The dataset also includes over 150 columns which are not needed for our analysis. Below we also subset the data so that we only see the columns we care about.

# add the conference variable
data["conference"] = (
    data["Team"]
    .str.extract(r"\(([^()]*)\)\s*$", expand=False)
)

# add the win and loss variables
data[["wins", "losses"]] = (
    data["Win-Loss"]
    .str.extract(r"^\s*(\d+)\s*-\s*(\d+)\s*$")
    .astype("Int64")
)

# calculate the win percentage
data["win_pct"] = (
    data["wins"] /
    (data["wins"] + data["losses"])
)

## check things worked by looking at just the selected columns head and tail
# select specific columns to use
check_cols = [
    "Team",
    "conference",
    "Win-Loss",
    "wins",
    "losses", 
    "win_pct"
]


# take all rows and just the columns in check_cols
football = data.loc[:, check_cols].copy()

We can see that the SEC is the top conference, in terms of win percentage. This is not the most accurate or best way to evaluate top conference but it can be used as a piece of an analysis. We will not analyze other metrics to evaluate the best conference. Instead, let’s plot the analysis we have done!
Below we plot these top 15 teams.

top_teams_plot = top_15_teams.sort_values("win_pct").plot.barh(
    x = "Team",
    y = "win_pct",
    legend = False
)

top_teams_plot.set_title("Top 15 College Football Teams by Win Percentage (2023)")
top_teams_plot.set_xlabel("Win Percentage")
top_teams_plot.set_ylabel("Team")








We can see that all of our top 15 teams are over 0.5 win percentage which would make sense for top teams. It is also important to see that there are many ties in the data since generally teams play the same amount of games each season leading to the percentages being the same.
Next let’s look at the top conferences plot.

conferences = conference_summary.sort_values("win_pct", ascending = False).plot.bar(
    x = "conference",
    y = "win_pct",
    legend = False
)

conferences.set_title("College Football Conferences by Average Win Percentage (2023)")
conferences.set_xlabel("Conference")
conferences.set_ylabel("Win Percentage")








This is just a nice way of visually comparing conferences average win percentages.
Here we see that matplotlib is structured differently than a ggplot. matplotlib actually works a little bit closer to base R plotting. In ggplot, we use the + to add different elements of a plot. In base R you start a plot and then can add things to the plot after the plot is intitialized. This is the same idea for matplotlib.

title: Tidyverse to Pandas: A How to Guide to Transition from R to Python
text: For many statistics students, we first learned R or did Python briefly. Stat 250 taught us to love the tidyverse with its ease of data wrangling. It allowed us to use the pipes |> and %>%, as well as the plain English functions select() and filter(). When we now need to learn Python, the switch can be daunting and throw us some curveballs and many errors. Python keeps throwing AttributeError and ValueError at us and we don’t know what to do. The challenge comes from the way Python and R handle data structures. Python handles data structures through an object-oriented lens as compared to R which handles data through a functional lens. In R, functions work on data frames whereas in Python, DataFrames are objects with their own methods and attributes. This tutorial is here to bridge this gap. We will walk through importing, cleaning, and exploring a real-world sports dataset in pandas, work through the most frequent syntax stumbling blocks, provide a handy comparison table, and equip you to write your own clean Python code without syntax errors.

Notice the syntax pattern: rather than passing the dataset into a standalone function like tail(data, 6), our DataFram data calls its own method .tail(6).
Next, let’s inspect the dimensions of the table.

data.shape

(134, 152)


Here is our first major conceptual difference: .shape does not take parenthenses (). In Python, data.shape is an attribute, not a method. Calling data.shape() will raise a TypeError: 'tuple' object is not callable.
To check for missing values across all columns, we can chain two methods:

# count number of na's for each variable
data.isna().sum()

Unnamed: 0                      0
Off Rank                        0
Team                            0
Games                           0
Win-Loss                        0
                               ..
Fumbles Lost                    0
Interceptions Thrown_y          0

In R, we might write colSums(is.na(data)). In pandas, .isna() generates a boolean mask of True and False values, and .sum() adds them up along each column (True = 1 and False = 0). Notice how when we chain multiple methods we add each one to the end of the last rather than nesting functions together like in R.

text:
Data Cleaning and Wrangling
Our raw data set contains 152 columns, most of which are not needed for our analysis. We want to be able to evaluate team and conference performance based on win percentages and conference affliation.
However, there is not column for conference and instead the conference is embedded in the team column and wins and losses are grouped in the same column. Each come with unique formatting issues:

The conference is trapped inside the raw Team column wrapped in parentheses (e.g., "Michigan (Big 10)).
Wins and losses are stored together in the Win-Loss column as a string separated by a hyphen (e.g., "15-0").

Just like using stringr in R, pandas provides a vectorized .str attribute to perform regular expression extractions:

# add the conference variable
data["conference"] = (
    data["Team"]
    .str.extract(r"\(([^()]*)\)\s*$", expand=False)
)

# add the win and loss variables
data[["wins", "losses"]] = (
    data["Win-Loss"]
    .str.extract(r"^\s*(\d+)\s*-\s*(\d+)\s*$")
    .astype("Int64")
)

# calculate the win percentage
data["win_pct"] = (
    data["wins"] /
    (data["wins"] + data["losses"])
)

## check things worked by looking at just the selected columns head and tail
# select specific columns to use
check_cols = [
    "Team",
    "conference",
    "Win-Loss",
    "wins",
    "losses", 
    "win_pct"
]


# take all rows and just the columns in check_cols
# subset rows and columns using .loc and create a copy of the data.
football = data.loc[:, check_cols].copy()

title: Tidyverse to Pandas: A How to Guide to Transition from R to Python
text:
Visualizing Results
In R, ggplot2 builds plots additively with + layers.
Conveniently, pandas DataFrames can directly generate matplotlib plots using their built in .plot method:

top_teams_plot = top_15_teams.sort_values("win_pct").plot.barh(
    x = "Team",
    y = "win_pct",
    legend = False
)

top_teams_plot.set_title("Top 15 College Football Teams by Win Percentage (2023)")
top_teams_plot.set_xlabel("Win Percentage")
top_teams_plot.set_ylabel("Team")








Let’s do the same for the conference averages:

conferences = conference_summary.sort_values("win_pct", ascending = False).plot.bar(
    x = "conference",
    y = "win_pct",
    legend = False
)

conferences.set_title("College Football Conferences by Average Win Percentage (2023)")
conferences.set_xlabel("Conference")
conferences.set_ylabel("Win Percentage")








Unlike ggplot2’s use of grammar layers, matplotlib operates via an Object-Oriented interface. When you call .plot(), pandas returns an Axes object (named here as top_teams_plot or conferences), and we configure labels, titles, and layout by calling methods on that axis. This is pretty similar in style to how base R plotting works.

title: Tidyverse to Pandas: A How to Guide to Transition from R to Python
section: Common Syntax Pitfalls When Switching Languages
text:
Common Syntax Pitfalls When Switching Languages
Beyond the worked example, here are some of the most frequent syntax hurdles encountered when switching from R to Python.

1. Booleans and Case Sensitivity
In R, for booleans we capitalize the whole word (i.e. TRUE). In Python, we only capitalize the first letter (i.e. True). Typing TRUE in Python triggers a NameError: name 'TRUE' is not defined.


2. 0-Based vs. 1-Based Indexing
R begins indexing at 1, and slicing includes both boundaries: vec[1:5] returns elements 1, 2, 3, 4, and 5. Python uses 0-based indexing and excludes the upper bound: vec[0:5] returns the first 5 elements (indices 0, 1, 2, 3, and 4). Remembering that Python counts from zero prevents off-by-one bugs.


3. Methods vs. Attributes (The Parentheses Trap)
In R, everything is executed via a function call with parentheses (e.g., dim(df), names(df)). In Python, objects store metadata as attributes accessed without parentheses.

df.shape (not df.shape()) returns (rows, columns) as a tuple.
df['col'].dtype (not df['col'].dtype() or type()) returns the column data type.
Methods that actively perform computations like df.head() or df.describe() require parentheses.



4. Vectorized Logic: Bitwise &, |, ~ vs. Scalar and, or, not
This is arguably the most common error for transitioning students. In R, logical operators like &, |, and ! are vectorized across entire columns by default.
In Python:

and, or, and not evaluate whether an entire container as a single entity is truthy or falsy. If you run df[(df['wins'] > 10) and (df['losses'] == 0)], Python halts with: ValueError: The truth value of a Series is ambiguous.
To filter element-wise across a pandas Series, you must use bitwise operators: & (AND), | (OR), and ~ (NOT).
Because bitwise operators have higher operator precedence than comparison operators (>, <), you must wrap each condition in parentheses:
# Correct pandas filtering syntax:
undefeated = football[(football["wins"] > 10) & (football["losses"] == 0)]



5. for Loops, and if Statements
In R we construct a for loop by doing:
for (variable in seq) { 
    #code for each iteration
}
In Python we construct a for loop by doing:
for variable in iterable:
    #code for each iteration
    # make sure it is idented
In R we construct an if statment by doing:
if (condition){
    # whatever you want to happen
} else if (condition 2){
    # whatever you want to happen
} else{
    # whatever you want to happen
}
In Python we construct an if statment by doing:
if condition: 
    # indented whatever you want to happen
elif condition: 
    # indented whatever you want to happen
else: 
    # indented whatever you want to happen
